demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
Kwame is a 55-year-old married African American man who has made his living for decades as a painter, moving between residential jobs and commercial interiors, accustomed to long hours on ladders, the smell of primer, and the steady satisfaction of leaving a room transformed. Before the death of his loved one, he understood himself as dependable, practical, and able to keep going through difficulty. He now speaks about life as divided into before and after.

The death came unexpectedly and with a violence that still feels unfinished to him. His loved one collapsed suddenly at home. Kwame remembers the rush of trying to understand what was happening, the helplessness of being in the house while everything changed in minutes, and the arrival of the ambulance. What remains with him most vividly are not smooth, complete memories but stark visual fragments: emergency lights flashing against the walls, the shape of people moving quickly through the house, the sight of his loved one being taken away, the doorway, the stretcher. At other times there is no picture at all, only the full force of the moment crashing back into him. He described episodes in which grief hits with such intensity that for a few seconds it is as if his body has remembered something his mind cannot fully bring into view. When he does deliberately recall the day, he is overwhelmed by grief so quickly that he often stops himself mid-thought.

In the months after the death, these experiences began threading themselves into ordinary parts of his life. Because his work takes him into other people's homes and around active neighborhoods, he cannot fully control what he encounters. If an ambulance passes a job site with its siren on, he feels his whole body tighten at once. He becomes rigid, watchful, and distracted, his attention pulled away from the wall in front of him. Even being at work itself has become loaded. Standing in a room with drop cloths spread out and paint supplies arranged, he can suddenly feel a wave of emotion that seems to come from nowhere and everywhere at once, as though the ordinary act of working has become entangled with the day his own home turned into an emergency scene. On some jobs, clients talk casually about illness, funerals, or someone "losing a loved one," and he feels himself shut down internally. He does not experience those conversations as sympathetic small talk; to him they land with a rawness that makes it hard to stay present.

At home, where he once expected comfort, Kwame has found himself unable to settle. Night is especially difficult. He says it is harder to feel safe after dark than during the day, and his body rarely seems to stand down from readiness. He notices his muscles staying tense, his breathing becoming shallow, and a constant sense that he must be prepared to react, though he cannot say to what. He checks the house more than he used to and remains alert even in familiar rooms. His wife has noticed that he does not fully relax into the couch in the evenings and that he listens closely to sounds outside. Being inside his own home no longer guarantees the feeling of being protected.

As time has passed, Kwame has come to speak about himself in altered terms. He says he no longer knows who he is. The version of himself he trusted-the man who could handle what needed handling, who knew his place in his family and his work-feels inaccessible to him now. Around other people he often feels cut off, as if he has been moved into a separate category from everyone still living ordinary life. Even when he is with coworkers or beside his wife, there are moments when he feels profoundly apart, unable to imagine that they can understand the force of what returns to him. He has come to believe that the trauma destroyed his life, not only because of the loss itself but because the life that followed has felt unrecognizable.

This has had visible consequences. On painting jobs he has become quieter and more easily derailed when something in the environment reminds him of the death. At times he tries to avoid conversations that might turn toward bereavement, stepping away or changing the subject, which has made him seem distant to customers and less available to coworkers. At home, his guardedness has narrowed family life; evenings are less easy, and his wife experiences him as physically present but difficult to reach.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was the accumulation of these moments rather than a single crisis. He has grown frightened by how little peace he feels, especially at night, and by the sense that grief can overtake him without warning, sometimes as pictures and sometimes as pure emotional force. He is afraid that this is who he is now: a man permanently cut off from himself, from other people, and from any sense of safety. At the same time, he comes to treatment hoping there might still be some way to live in his home, do his work, and remember his loved one without feeling that each reminder destroys him all over again.
